meta.title: Marburg Watch
meta.description: Independent, sourced Marburg tracker: any new cases in Africa, Uganda's isolated case in 2026, and the full record of Ethiopia's first outbreak (November 2025 to January 2026) with a dated timeline.
meta.disclaimer: This tracker summarises reports from WHO, CDC, ECDC, UKHSA, Africa CDC and Ethiopia's Ministry of Health, and named news outlets. It is not medical or travel advice. If you develop a fever within 21 days of contact with someone who had Marburg, call a doctor before going to a clinic.

headline: No further Marburg cases have been reported since Uganda's isolated case in late June. Ethiopia's first outbreak ended on 26 January with 14 confirmed cases and 9 deaths.

status.label: Watching · no new cases reported
status.summary: Uganda notified WHO of a confirmed Marburg case in Kyegegwa district on 30 June 2026: a young child who had died, found through surveillance set up for Ebola. Africa CDC said no contacts had developed symptoms, and no further cases have been reported since. Ethiopia's first outbreak, confirmed in Jinka on 14 November 2025, was declared over on 26 January 2026 after 42 days without a new case. WHO counted 14 confirmed cases, 9 of whom died, plus 5 probable cases who all died. Headlines saying Ethiopia's death toll is climbing date from December 2025.

claims.claim: Ethiopia's Marburg death toll is still climbing
claims.detail: Headlines such as CIDRAP's 'Death toll climbs in Ethiopia's Marburg outbreak' date from early December 2025. The final count was 9 deaths among 14 confirmed cases, plus 5 probable cases who died, and the outbreak was declared over on 26 January 2026.

claims.claim: Marburg has returned to Ethiopia in 2026
claims.detail: This tracker found no official reports of Marburg cases in Ethiopia since the outbreak ended on 26 January 2026; the last confirmed case was reported on 12 December 2025. Uganda, not Ethiopia, reported a Marburg case in June 2026.

claims.claim: The virus in Ethiopia was a new strain
claims.detail: Genetic analysis by the Ethiopian Public Health Institute found the same strain reported in earlier outbreaks in East Africa, WHO and UKHSA said.

claims.claim: Marburg spread from Ethiopia to other countries
claims.detail: CDC reported no cases linked to this outbreak outside Ethiopia. Africa CDC said it was working to prevent spread to neighbouring countries, mainly South Sudan and Kenya.

claims.claim: There is an approved Marburg vaccine
claims.detail: No Marburg vaccine or treatment is licensed. Ethiopia tested Sabin's investigational cAd3-Marburg vaccine in a Phase 2 trial; when the outbreak ended, 227 people were enrolled in one group and 340 in a second, randomised group.

claims.claim: Health workers were among those infected
claims.detail: Three health workers were infected; two died and one recovered, WHO says. WHO cited infections among health workers when it rated the risk in Ethiopia high.

positions.text: Declared the outbreak over after 42 days without a new case. 14 people were confirmed infected: 9 died and 5 recovered.
14 confirmed and 5 probable cases as of 25 January; all probable cases died. Three health workers were infected, two of whom died. The outbreak was contained in less than three months.
14 confirmed cases and 9 deaths. No cases linked to the outbreak outside Ethiopia; the risk to the US is low.
No new confirmed cases in the past week. The source has not been identified, though fruit bats were found in the area. Risk to the UK public very low.
Coordinated efforts under way to prevent cross-border spread, mainly to South Sudan and Kenya.

timeline.title: First known patient admitted to hospital in Jinka
timeline.body: An adult from Jinka, later identified as the outbreak's first known case, is admitted to the town's general hospital with nausea and stomach cramps, according to South Africa's NICD. WHO says the outbreak began in October.

timeline.title: Suspected viral haemorrhagic fever reported in Jinka
timeline.body: Ethiopia's health ministry and public health institute report 8 suspected cases of viral haemorrhagic fever in Jinka town, South Ethiopia Region.

timeline.title: Ethiopia confirms its first Marburg outbreak
timeline.body: Tests at the Ethiopian Public Health Institute confirm Marburg virus, and the health ministry declares the country's first Marburg outbreak. Genetic analysis by the institute shows the same strain as in earlier East African outbreaks.

timeline.title: WHO rates the risk high in Ethiopia
timeline.body: 6 of 33 samples tested are confirmed, including 3 people who died. WHO rates the risk high nationally, moderate for the region and low globally, citing unsupervised burials and infections among health workers.

timeline.title: 10 confirmed cases and 5 deaths
timeline.body: The health ministry reports two more confirmed infections. Africa CDC says it is working to prevent spread across the borders, mainly to South Sudan and Kenya.

timeline.title: Death toll rises to six
timeline.body: Of 11 people with confirmed infection, 6 have died and 5 are being treated, the health ministry says.

timeline.title: Deaths reach eight; first case in Hawassa
timeline.body: 12 confirmed cases and 8 deaths; 3 patients have recovered and 349 contacts are being followed. A case is confirmed in Hawassa, Sidama region: a contact of an earlier case who had travelled to Jinka. CIDRAP reports these figures under the headline 'Death toll climbs in Ethiopia's Marburg outbreak'.

timeline.title: Vaccine trial begins; CDC alerts US clinicians
timeline.body: Sabin Vaccine Institute sends more than 640 doses of its investigational cAd3-Marburg vaccine for a Phase 2 trial, sponsored by Ethiopia's health ministry, at three health facilities. CDC issues a health advisory.

timeline.title: Last confirmed patient dies; 42-day countdown begins
timeline.body: The 14th and last confirmed case was reported on 12 December, bringing the total to 14 cases and 9 deaths. WHO's 42-day countdown to declaring the outbreak over starts on 14 December, after the death of the last confirmed patient.

timeline.title: CDC: no cases outside Ethiopia
timeline.body: CDC counts 14 confirmed cases and 9 deaths. No cases linked to the outbreak have been reported outside Ethiopia, and the risk to the US is low. CDC's most likely scenario was an outbreak of fewer than 30 cases.

timeline.title: Health ministry: 21 days without a new case
timeline.body: The ministry says no new case has been detected for 21 days and all contacts of the last patients have completed follow-up. About 3,800 people had been tested since November.

timeline.title: Ethiopia declares its first Marburg outbreak over
timeline.body: After 42 days without a new case, the health ministry declares the outbreak over, less than three months after it was confirmed. WHO counts 14 confirmed cases, of whom 9 died and 5 recovered, plus 5 probable cases who all died. Three health workers were infected; two died. Enhanced surveillance continues for 90 days.

timeline.title: WHO reviews its Marburg response in Ethiopia
timeline.body: WHO Ethiopia holds an internal review in Addis Ababa from 17 to 19 March. WHO notes early delays in detection and infections among health workers, and says its surge teams helped contain the outbreak quickly.

timeline.title: Uganda reports a Marburg case in Kyegegwa
timeline.body: Uganda notifies WHO of a confirmed Marburg case in Kyegegwa district, found through surveillance set up for Ebola. Africa CDC says the patient, a young child, had died and no contacts had symptoms. In mid-July WHO said it was still seeking updates from Uganda.

history.text: Angola's outbreak, centred on Uíge province, is the largest Marburg outbreak on record.
Equatorial Guinea and Tanzania (Kagera region) report their first Marburg outbreaks.
Rwanda's outbreak, detected in September, is declared over on 20 December after 42 days without a new case.
A second outbreak in Kagera, Tanzania. Genome sequencing compares its virus with the 2023 one.
Ethiopia's first outbreak: 14 confirmed cases and 9 deaths in South Ethiopia and Sidama regions. Declared over on 26 January 2026.
Uganda notifies WHO of a Marburg case in Kyegegwa district on 30 June, found through Ebola surveillance.

facts.a: A severe, often fatal viral haemorrhagic fever in the same virus family as Ebola. Fruit bats are the natural host: people can catch it from bats and then pass it to others. Past outbreaks have killed between 24% and 88% of patients.

facts.q: How does it spread between people?
facts.a: Through direct contact with the blood or other body fluids of someone who is sick with Marburg or has died of it, or with surfaces and materials contaminated by those fluids. Health workers and people who handle the bodies of those who died are at particular risk.

Illness starts suddenly with high fever, severe headache and extreme tiredness, often followed by vomiting, diarrhoea and stomach pain. Some patients bleed. Symptoms can appear up to 21 days after infection.

facts.q: Is there a vaccine or treatment?
facts.a: None is licensed. Early supportive care, such as fluids and treatment of symptoms, improves survival. During the outbreak Ethiopia ran a trial of Sabin's investigational cAd3-Marburg vaccine, and the US sent doses of an investigational vaccine and treatment.

facts.q: When is an outbreak declared over?
facts.a: After 42 days, two full 21-day incubation periods, with no new case following the recovery or safe burial of the last patient. Ethiopia's countdown began on 14 December 2025, and the outbreak was declared over on 26 January 2026.
